webrarian builds a whole R workspace as a website. Visitors get an editor, a
console, files, plots and an environment, with your packages and files ready
when the page opens, and they write and run their own code against what you
prepared.

![What a visitor gets, already set up. There is an editor (1), a console (2), the environment and files (3), plots and help (4), edits kept between visits (5) and an address of your choosing (6).](images/webr-browser.svg){#fig-workspace fig-alt="A browser window at my-analysis.netlify.app showing the workspace. Numbered callouts mark the editor holding analysis.R, the console after installing packages and running the script, the Files tab with the file tree under web_user, the Plots tab with a bar chart, the footer with Reset files, and the address bar"}

It suits four kinds of job.

- course materials where students start with the data and packages loaded
- a reproducible analysis readers can rerun and change
- a workshop sandbox with nothing to install
- an internal R console on a network without internet access

Four features set it apart.

- You build the site from R (`catalog()`, `acquire_package()`, `bind()`), with no
  HTML or JavaScript.
- Sites can be self-contained. With `build.offline: true` a site makes no
  request to another server, and `collection_mirror()` adds a package repository
  visitors can install from on closed networks.
- It compiles your local or GitHub packages (with Docker), or uses an
  r-universe that has built them.
- It sets up GitHub Pages and Netlify deployment, brands sites with brand.yml,
  and supports share links.

pyodidarian, the Python counterpart, is released separately.

## Other tools

No tool does everything, and webrarian is the wrong one for a Shiny app. The
table shows what each was built for.

| | webrarian | shinylive | quarto-live | webR REPL | JupyterLite |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Built for | a workspace site around your packages and files | Shiny apps | runnable cells in a Quarto document | an R console to use now | notebooks |
| How you make it | R functions and `_webrarian.yml` | `shinylive::export()` | a Quarto format | nothing to build | a JupyterLite build |
| Languages | R | R and Python | R and Python | R | Python, and R through xeus-r |

Here is each in a sentence.

- [shinylive](https://posit-dev.github.io/r-shinylive/) runs Shiny apps in the
  browser, which the webrarian workspace does not.
- [quarto-live](https://r-wasm.github.io/quarto-live/) makes code blocks in a
  Quarto document runnable, for tutorials where the prose leads.
- The [webR REPL](https://webr.r-wasm.org/latest/) is webR's own console,
  ready with nothing to build. webrarian adds your packages and files to a
  site you host.
- [JupyterLite](https://jupyterlite.readthedocs.io/) runs notebooks, and R runs
  there through xeus-r with packages from emscripten-forge rather than
  repo.r-wasm.org.

They combine well. A Quarto course can use quarto-live for lessons and link to
a webrarian workspace for assignments.
